agent.problem: Detail-heavy tabernacle building stretches are still handled item by item. The clearest example is stop 2, cards 8-12, where the lampstand details in Exodus 37:17-24 become two story cards and three choice cards about almond blossoms, one-piece construction and the number of lamps. Similar quizzing over loop counts and base metals appears in stop 1. These stretches should be summarized concisely rather than used for multiple choice cards.

rule.text: The rule: Papa Dorin sums up the stretch in one story card. A short story inside the stretch, like Nimrod in the list of nations (Genesis 10:8–12), is part of the stretch: it can be the standout detail on that card, but it gets no choice cards. A stretch never gets a stop of its own. Its one card sits in the stop with the moments around it. He says in a few words what it covers and doesn't go item by item. He can name a standout detail the text gives if it helps the stretch stick. The baker should know the stretch is there and what it's about, not memorize it. A long stretch never gets a choice card.

agent.problem: The question specifies that the bases are a metal, but the wrong answer "Stone" is not a metal. It is therefore immediately eliminated by the setup and is not the same kind of answer as "Bronze" and "Gold."

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

agent.problem: Too much of this stop depends on guessing unseen details. The horn at each corner (card 2), the mirrors used for the basin (card 8), Bezalel's tribe (card 12) and Oholiab's tribe (card 13) cannot be reasoned out from the earlier cards. The mirror question could serve as one discovery question, but with the horn and two tribal-affiliation questions, most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question. A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

human.problem: Almost this whole passage (Exodus 36:8-38:31) is building plans for the tabernacle, its furnishings and its courtyard, followed by a material count. The docs list building plans like this as a long stretch. A long stretch gets one summary card, no choice cards and never a stop of its own. The walkthrough uses that treatment for the frames, the courtyard and the totals, but gives the curtains, the ark, the table, the lampstand and the altars many detail choice cards, such as which metal the clasps and bases are made of.
human.question: When an entire passage is a long stretch, like the building chapters of the tabernacle, how should Prep handle it? Which parts count as moments worth choice cards, and which parts get the one-card summary treatment?

human.problem: Almost the whole passage is construction detail: curtain counts and sizes, loops, clasps, frames, bases, furnishings and courtyard measurements. prep-walkthrough.md lists building plans for the tabernacle as a long stretch, which gets one summary story card and never a choice card. The walkthrough summarizes only two parts this way (36:20-34 and 38:9-20). It asks choice cards on other build details of the same kind, such as goat hair curtain counts, loop counts and base metals (stop 1 cards 6, 7, 13, 14).
human.question: When a whole passage, or nearly all of it, is the kind of detail the docs call a long stretch (here, the tabernacle being built), how should Prep handle it? A stretch can't have a stop of its own or any choice cards, but Prep still needs stops with at least as many choice cards as story cards. Which build details, if any, may get choice cards, and which must be folded into summary story cards?
